subject: research/ambient-hlrtlevel
professional: a statistician who works on likelihood-ratio tests in latent-class / mixture models and Monte Carlo tests (a referee for JASA, Biometrika or Statistics and Computing); first checks: are the reported intervals right, is the null fit a true MLE, is the Monte Carlo p-value constructed so its null law is known, is the simulation big enough to answer the question, and is the result new against McLachlan's bootstrap LRT literature

evidence.correctness: Recomputed outside the author's code (scratchpad hlrt/indep.py, gen.py; Python 3.13 + SciPy 1.18). (1) All six Clopper-Pearson intervals in the README table from scipy beta quantiles: 11/200 [0.028, 0.096], 9/200 [0.021, 0.084], 8/200 [0.017, 0.077], 20/200 [0.062, 0.150], 16/200 [0.046, 0.127], 19/200 [0.058, 0.144], identical to experiments/results.txt; the earlier 7/60 gives [0.048, 0.226], so finding 2 ('0.117 outside this run's interval but inside the earlier run's own') holds. (2) The null-model MLE: my own direct L-BFGS maximisation of the h = 0 log-likelihood (softmax parameters, 5 random starts) matches fit_null's EM log-likelihood per message to within 4e-8 at n = 100, 200, 500. (3) The data generator draw3_hard at h = 0 against my own analytic joint sum_t pi_t A A A C on 400,000 messages: chi-square over 81 cells 79.9, p = 0.48. (4) The exact null law of the B = 39 Monte Carlo p-value: P(p <= 0.05) = 2/40 = 0.05, P(p <= 0.10) = 4/40 = 0.10, so the nominal rates the table compares with are right; E[p] = 41/80 = 0.5125, not 0.5. (5) Reran the author's experiment unchanged from a scratch cwd (same seeds): the n = 100 row reproduced exactly (11/200, 20/200, mean p 0.495); the n = 200 and 500 rows also reproduced exactly (9/200, 16/200, 0.524; 8/200, 19/200, 0.523), about 31 minutes wall on 4 cores.
evidence.completeness: What the README says is done: 4 tests (4 pass), the 200-draw x 3-n experiment (rerun, reproduces), the figure (experiments/level.png present, shows the three empirical p CDFs on the diagonal), the Clopper-Pearson helper checked against its defining property (test present). Live page not loaded (proxy 403 for marisstella.app); research/README.md bullet and _homepage entry match the results. Nothing claimed is missing; the follow-up the parent asked for (more draws for the level) was done only for n in {100, 200, 500}, not the n = 1000 cell that was the other half of the parent's anomaly.
evidence.verification: `PYTHONPATH=src /usr/bin/python3.13 -m pytest -q tests`: 4 passed in 0.23 s. Three tests cover the 18-line Clopper-Pearson helper; the only test of the LRT and bootstrap is that p lies in [0.25, 1] and T >= 0 with B = 3. Five seeded mutants via quality_mutate.py: caught 1 (Clopper-Pearson alpha/2 -> alpha); survived 4: fit_null's shared-matrix update 's(ta)+s(tb)+s(tc)' -> 's(ta)' (a wrong null MLE), p = (1+exceed)/(B+1) -> (1+exceed)/B, T* >= T -> T* > T, and 2n -> n in the statistic (the last two are near-equivalent for the p-value, but the first two change the headline). No test compares the null fit with an independent optimiser, the statistic with a hand case, or the bootstrap with a case of known null law.
evidence.craft: Read src/ambient_hlrtlevel/{est,stats,sim}.py, tests/test_level.py, experiments/run.py. stats.py is clean (bisection on the binomial cdf, 60 halvings) and run.py is short and seeded with disjoint seed streams per n (residues 9, 5, 6 mod 13). But est.py is a verbatim 369-line copy of ambient-hlrt's (diff: identical), itself a copy of earlier projects, of which about 300 lines (naive, EM, two-auditor and plain DS, multistart, start-count helpers) are unused here; sim.py is likewise copied and unused except for constants; sample_null keeps an unused 'acc_unused' parameter. Copied engines across a chain of slugs (ambient-hlrt -> hlrtlevel -> hlrtmis) instead of one shared package.
evidence.claims: Checked: table numbers vs experiments/results.txt (all 15 match), and vs my rerun (n = 100 identical); CI values (scipy, identical); 'every interval contains 0.05 / 0.10' (true); finding 2 hedged as 'a reading, not a test' (fair); finding 3 'a true level of 0.08 would not be ruled out' (P(X <= 11 | 200, 0.08) = 0.117, true); smallest attainable p 1/40 (true); 4 tests (true); stylised disclosure and AI note present; limitations list misspecification, B and power. One soft overclaim: 'mean p is near 0.5, as for a uniform p-value' - the valid-test expectation with B = 39 is 0.5125 and the observed 0.495-0.524 straddle it; harmless but the benchmark is stated wrong. Runtime claim 'about 40 minutes on 4 cores' consistent with my rerun (31 min).
evidence.fitness: Job: a researcher wants to know whether the parametric-bootstrap LRT of 'no hard class' in a three-annotator Dawid-Skene-with-hardness model can be trusted for size. Nearest prior work: McLachlan (1987, Applied Statistics 36:318-324) on bootstrapping the LRT for the number of mixture components, Feng and McCulloch (1996, JRSS B) on its consistency, Chen, Chen and Kalbfleisch's modified LRT / EM test for mixtures, and Monte Carlo test theory (Hope 1968; Davison and Hinkley 1997, ch. 4). That the parametric bootstrap holds its level when the generator matches the null is the expected textbook result; with 200 draws and B = 39 the run can only exclude gross failures (+/-0.03). The useful follow-ups - the n = 1000 cell where the parent saw 0/60, misspecified nulls, a parameter sweep - are not here (the next slug, ambient-hlrtmis, does misspecification). A researcher can reuse the code; the result is a sanity check, not a publishable finding, and is not part of any programme in PROGRAMMES.md (legacy slug).
evidence.domain: Sound practice: Monte Carlo p = (1 + #{T* >= T})/(B + 1) (Davison-Hinkley 4.2), refitting both models on every bootstrap draw, clipping T at 0, exact binomial intervals for the rejection rate, a calibration plot of the whole p CDF rather than one level. Departs from what a referee expects: B = 39 is the minimum that makes p <= 0.05 attainable; Davison and Hinkley recommend at least 99 for a 5% test and the power loss of small B (Jockel 1986) matters for the parent's power claims; no citation of the bootstrap-LRT-for-mixtures literature, which already establishes the method and its pitfalls; all inputs are round numbers at one point (auditor 0.8, classifier 0.7, one prior), with no sweep, contrary to research/CLAUDE.md 'run the numbers'; only 2 starts for the alternative, so a search miss biases T low on both the observed and bootstrap fits (it cancels in the level, but is not checked).

defects.what: The LRT and bootstrap that the headline rests on are effectively untested: the only test checks 0.25 <= p <= 1 with B = 3; seeded mutants that break the null MLE update (shared-matrix counts from one auditor only) or the p-value denominator ((1+exceed)/B) leave all 4 tests green.

The follow-up re-examines only the parent's n = 200 anomaly (7/60); the parent's other level estimate, 0/60 at n = 1000 (a possibly conservative test, which is what would cost power), is cited in the README's first line but n = 1000 is not among the sizes run.

No prior work on the method: the parametric bootstrap LRT for the number of mixture/latent-class components is McLachlan (1987) with Feng and McCulloch (1996) on its validity, and Monte Carlo test size with small B is Hope (1968) / Davison and Hinkley (1997); the result (level holds when the generator matches the null) is the expected one and its novelty is not placed against them.

Every driving input is a single round figure (auditor accuracy 0.8, classifier 0.7, one class prior) with no sweep, so the level conclusion is shown at one point only; research/CLAUDE.md asks for a sweep when no sourced figure exists.

'mean p is near 0.5, as for a uniform p-value': with B = 39 a valid Monte Carlo p is uniform on {1,...,40}/40, mean 41/80 = 0.5125, not 0.5; the observed 0.495-0.524 are near either, but the stated benchmark is wrong.
est.py is a verbatim 369-line copy of ambient-hlrt's (itself copied down a chain of slugs) of which about 300 lines are unused here; sample_null keeps an unused acc_unused parameter.

B = 39 is the smallest B for which p <= 0.05 is attainable; Davison and Hinkley recommend B >= 99 for a 5% test, and small B loses power (disclosed as a limitation, but kept as the recommended practice in the parent's 'about 40 refits is enough').

verdict: The numbers are right and reproduce: rerunning the author's experiment with its seeds gives the README table exactly at n = 100, 200 and 500, my own SciPy Clopper-Pearson intervals match all six, my own L-BFGS null MLE matches fit_null to 4e-8, the generator passes a chi-square against my analytic joint (p = 0.48), and the B = 39 Monte Carlo p has null law 0.05 / 0.10 as the table assumes. It does not meet the bar: 4 of 5 seeded mutants in the LRT/bootstrap core survive (only the 18-line interval helper is tested), and as research it is a 200-draw sanity check at one round-number parameter point that confirms the textbook expectation (parametric bootstrap holds size when the model is right) without citing McLachlan (1987) or the Monte Carlo test literature, and without revisiting the parent's n = 1000 cell (0/60). Claims are honest and hedged; the one slip is comparing mean p with 0.5 instead of 0.5125.
